claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native iron-oxide surface layer.
The native oxide contains phases such as Fe3O4 and Fe2O3.
At room temperature, the native oxide limits oxygen and salt-ion ingress and therefore protects Q235 steel.
At 700–900 °C in salt-containing environments, thermal-expansion mismatch destabilizes the native oxide.
Accelerated oxide growth at 700–900 °C destabilizes the native oxide.
High-temperature destabilization produces a thicker, porous, and spalled oxide scale.
Porosity and spallation permit aggressive species to reach the underlying metal and accelerate corrosion.
Commercial pre-exposure Q235 steel typically has a ferrite-pearlite microstructure.
At room temperature, the oxide scale is thin and adherent.
At high temperature, thermal stresses make the oxide scale porous or cause it to spall.
Rapid oxide growth combined with thermal-expansion mismatch generates microcracks and porosity.
Room-temperature salt exposure will produce minimal mass change and limited corrosion in Q235 steel with intact native oxide.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce significantly greater mass change than room-temperature exposure.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce observable oxide spallation and increased scale porosity.
Aggressive ions will infiltrate the high-temperature oxide scale.
Removing the native oxide before exposure provides a control for determining the role of the pre-existing oxide.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to as-received Q235 steel retaining its original oxide layer.
The mechanism may not apply to steels with engineered oxide scales, Cr or Ni alloying additions, or prior thermal treatments that alter oxide characteristics.

contradictions.description: The study requires identical surface finish for all samples while also comparing native-oxide-preserved specimens with specimens polished to remove that oxide; polishing necessarily changes surface finish as well as oxide state, creating a confound unless roughness and preparation are separately controlled.

The design claims to isolate temperature, but the room-temperature test may use a salt atmosphere or spray chamber whereas the high-temperature test uses furnace exposure with deposited salt. Differences in salt delivery, atmosphere, and wet versus dry exposure prevent temperature from being the sole changed variable.
